item.title: Any site can frame Harvard's pages.
item.description:
Organization JSON-LD, a sitemap index, and Core Web Vitals that pass for real visitors. But the pages analyzed send neither X-Frame-Options nor frame-ancestors, so another site could load them in a hidden frame.
The lesson for every team: Send Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'. It blocks clickjacking and replaces X-Frame-Options.
One automated analysis of public pages on 19 Oct 2026. A starting point, not a verdict. How the review works, step by step: https://carlosandmunoz.com/qa-review-guide.html?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=runs-100-2026-11&utm_content=harvard
#WebSecurity #Clickjacking #HigherEd #QA #QAlab

item.title: Node.js has llms.txt. Its pages share a pitch.
item.description:
An llms.txt for AI tools, security.txt, preloaded HSTS, and two sitemaps. But 19 of the 20 pages analyzed share one meta description, the home page's, so Learn and About pitch the same line in search.
The lesson for every team: Write a description per page that says what that page answers. A shared one tells search nothing new.

item.description:

item.title: Stanford's canonical leads to a 404.
item.description:
Preloaded HSTS, a nonce-based content security policy, a Permissions-Policy, and framing denied: Security 86. But the home page names stanford.edu/home as canonical, and that URL answers 404.
The lesson for every team: Fetch every canonical URL in your test suite. It should answer 200 and name itself as canonical.

item.title: El País sends no security headers.
item.description:

The lesson for every team: Start with four headers: Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, frame-ancestors, and a report-only CSP.

item.title: Le Monde has a CSP that allows any https.
item.description:
A year of HSTS, framing limited to its own origin, and NewsMediaOrganization JSON-LD. Its content security policy exists, but default-src allows any https: source plus 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval'.
The lesson for every team: List the script hosts you actually use, then drop 'unsafe-eval'. A policy that allows everything blocks nothing.

item.title: Your Lighthouse score is not your visitors.
item.description:
30-second trick: Your Lighthouse score is not your visitors.
PageSpeed Insights shows two things. The top half is real-user data from the Chrome UX Report over the last 28 days. The score below it is one lab run on a simulated phone.
Try it now: Read the top half first. If your page has no real-user data there, collect your own with Google's web-vitals library.
